description: We are Team Pinnacles, a two-member team of Computer Science undergraduates based in India. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are building Marswalk Planner, a human-scale terrain exploration and EVA route-planning tool for Jezero Crater on Mars. Our interests lie in space exploration, planetary science, geospatial data, AI, and applying technology to solve challenges in future space missions.
summary:
Marswalk Planner turns NASA's regional Mars data into something an astronaut could actually walk. We built a hyperlocal EVA planner for 3.08 x 2.07 km of Jezero crater's western delta front at 1 metre resolution, serving one science question: did the delta-front carbonates form in a standing lake, or by later groundwater alteration?

A map cannot answer that - only a sample can. So the tool works out where that sample must come from, and whether a crew can get there and back. It layers a HiRISE stereo DTM, CRISM carbonate detections, THEMIS thermal data, MOLA crater context, Perseverance's traverse, measured MEDA weather and live DONKI solar activity, then solves a least-cost route to three targets chosen for standable ground beside exposed carbonate-bearing rock more than 150 m from anywhere the rover drove.

Its core safety output is walk-back margin: standing anywhere in the area, is there still enough in the pack to reach the start? Endurance comes from Apollo flight data, not assumption. Every value on screen is badged MEASURED, DERIVED or ASSUMED from a provenance file the pipeline writes, so the app cannot cite a source it did not fetch.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Live app: https://marswalk-planner-six.vercel.app
Github repo: https://github.com/Roshan-1024?tab=repositories

Marswalk Planner presents Jezero's delta front as a 3D isometric diorama - a rotatable, zoomable slice of real Martian ground, not a flat map. It renders 3.08 x 2.07 km from a HiRISE stereo DTM at 1 m, drapes HiRISE imagery over the true topography, and lets you orbit, tilt and zoom the terrain while routes, hazard masks and mineral detections are painted directly onto the landscape they describe.

Over that diorama it solves a least-cost walking route with A* on a slope-derived cost surface. Three science targets are selected by four simultaneous criteria: standable ground under 20 degrees, an exposed face over 25 degrees within 30 m, a CRISM carbonate detection within 60 m, and more than 150 m from any point Perseverance drove. That last rule is the point - these are outcrops a rover could not reach, which is the case for sending people.

A 3D MARS EXPLORER, FROM THE ASTRONAUT'S PERSPECTIVE

One click drops you off the diorama and onto the surface itself. You become the astronaut: a 1.85 m suited crew member at true scale, standing on the same measured terrain, free to walk it in first or third person with WASD and mouse look.

This is not a flythrough. You walk at the pace the metabolic cost model dictates, so steep ground genuinely slows you down. The slope veto physically refuses to let you step onto terrain the router rejected. A navigation minimap lets you teleport anywhere in the area, the sun sits where NASA's Mars24 algorithm says it sits for that latitude and season - including sunset and night - and your walk-back margin updates with every step.

Vertical exaggeration is forced to 1.0 the moment you step down, because walking a 2.5x slope would misrepresent the one thing the mode exists to convey: what this ground is actually like. Scale is the argument. A 1.85 m human is 0.06% of the scene width, and the route is 5.7 km of that.

WALK-BACK MARGIN

Not "is the route walkable" but "standing here, is there still enough left to reach the start?" One Dijkstra sweep from the EVA start gives the fastest safe return from every cell (98.3% reachable, 62 min furthest), so the answer holds off-route too - and it draws over the diorama as 10-minute return isochrones. Endurance is Apollo's: the PLSS was designed for 4 h at 1200 Btu/hr and consumables deplete in proportion to metabolic rate. Resting metabolism is derived from the MET definition, not chosen. Tightest margin on our route: 105 minutes.

HONESTY AS A DESIGN CONSTRAINT

Every value is badged MEASURED, DERIVED or ASSUMED from provenance.json. We found four defects in the source data and handled each differently: imagery 95 m out of registration (corrected), the DTM floating ~12 m vertically (measured, deliberately NOT corrected, since slope and ascent are differences), a duplicate CRISM band (dropped), and a candidate basemap 28% truncated at source (rejected). One validation check passes; one is inconclusive and reported as such. Our own metabolic rate is reported as sitting ABOVE the band Apollo crews averaged.

TOOLS

Python (numpy, scipy, Pillow) for the data pipeline - PDS3 label parsing, HTTP range requests to pull only needed bytes from multi-GB products, image registration by cross-correlation, Horn slope, Dijkstra and A*. TypeScript, React, three.js and react-three-fiber for the diorama and the first-person explorer, with routing in a Web Worker. Solar geometry implements the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm, unit-tested against both published worked examples. 52 Python and 32 TypeScript tests. Apache 2.0.

CREATIVITY

The challenge notes NASA data is regional, not hyperlocal. Rather than build another Mars globe, we went the other way: one small area at the scale a person actually moves, every layer harmonised onto a single 1 m grid, presented first as a diorama you can study from above and then as ground you can stand on. Those are the two scales an EVA is planned at, and the same measured terrain serves both - the planner's cost model is the walker's walking speed. We also made the tool argue for its own numbers rather than assert them.
